key_facts: US regulators (FCC) approved SpaceX's plan to launch up to a million satellites into orbit to build orbital data centres, described as the first approval of its kind.
The project, known as Starmind, would use solar power in orbit to process AI data and send results back to Earth; FCC said it will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Under the licence, deployment must begin no later than November 2033, with 10% deployed by November 2035 and 50% by November 2038; SpaceX plans to launch its first Starmind satellite next year. It is unclear whether a million satellites will actually be launched.

Experts cited by the BBC say launching and protecting orbital hardware remains expensive, with space debris and collision risk among the concerns; Google and Blue Origin are also exploring orbital data centres.
importance_reason: Regulatory approval of a speculative, long-horizon infrastructure project with no direct near-term market impact; mainly a sector/tech story.
market_link: Possible long-term demand signal for space and satellite infrastructure and AI compute, but the effect on listed markets is not clear from the source.

region: Germany / EU (dispute involves US company Fender and German retailer Thomann)
key_facts: Fender Stratocaster body shape, designed in the US in the early 1950s and not trademarked when first made, is subject to a copyright dispute: a Düsseldorf court in December 2025 granted Fender copyright protection for the design in Germany in a default judgment, as the Chinese defendant Yiwu Philharmonic did not appear.

In March 2026 Fender sent cease-and-desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers demanding they stop making and selling Strat-style guitars for Germany and other EU countries, regardless of where produced. In June, Thomann filed an 'action of non-infringement'; in July, Fender sued Thomann in a German court for copyright infringement.
Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars in 2025, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and its subsidiary Squier.
importance_reason: Feature-style story about an IP dispute in the musical instruments retail sector with no direct market, macro or price impact.

key_facts: The UK government and the EU are set to publish texts of two treaties on Thursday afternoon, agreed last week as part of a new UK-EU deal, along with UK legislation (the Cutting Costs Bill) to enact the bulk of the deal.

The treaties reportedly contain a 10-year termination clause: if one party ends the agreement within that period, it would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which has been significantly scaled back under the new deal. Badenoch and Farage have suggested they would refuse to pay.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports; the BBC notes the cost reduction may not be visible to consumers at the checkout.

The treaties will affect UK aviation and maritime industries through alignment with EU emissions schemes; the legislation includes secondary legislation powers (so-called 'Henry VIII powers') for ministers to align UK and EU laws.
importance_reason: Significant UK-EU trade and regulatory development with sectoral effects, but no direct rate decision or market-moving price shock.
market_link: Potential effects on UK food exporters, aviation and maritime sectors via reduced border costs and alignment with EU emissions trading; the 16% agri-export forecast is an internal estimate cited by the BBC, not a confirmed outcome.

region: US / China / Vietnam / India / EU / South Korea / Taiwan / Singapore
actors: Singapore Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry
key_facts: The Trump administration proposed new tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity: starting at 15% for the EU, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan, rising to as much as 35% for Vietnam. China faces a capped rate of 20% on top of an existing 25% tariff; the rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January.

India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, which could fall to 17% and 20% if reciprocal trade agreements are concluded. Singapore faces a maximum potential rate of 20%, which could fall to 10% with a reciprocal trade agreement. The USTR says new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying duties could take effect as early as January.

Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to 'rectify its wrongdoing' and urged implementation of $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed in late September. Semiconductors and other electronics are excluded from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs, which analysts say cushions South Korea and Taiwan.
importance_reason: Новый пакет тарифов на более чем дюжину торговых партнёров США с потенциальной ставкой до 35–40% и прямым эффектом для торговли с Китаем, Вьетнамом и Индией.
market_link: Потенциальное повышение тарифов до 40% на китайские товары и 35% на вьетнамские может повлиять на торговые потоки, курсы валют азиатских экономик и цепочки поставок полупроводников и электроники.

key_facts: Администрация Трампа предложила ввести дополнительные импортные пошлины на товары 14 торговых партнёров, включая Китай и ЕС; обоснование — «перепроизводство» и государственные субсидии, искажающие мировую торговлю.

По данным Folha de S.Paulo, USTR объявило меры в среду; правительство Бразилии не получало предварительного уведомления. Предложено изменить пошлины на импорт бразильского сахара и авиатехники (Бруна Сантос оценивает пошлину на самолеты как «десятипроцентную»).

WSJ отмечает, что объявление совпало с трёхлетним максимумом одного из ключевых показателей инфляции и через несколько недель после поражения Республиканской партии на промежуточных выборах; 65% опрошенных избирателей заявили, что тарифы нанесли ущерб экономике.
China Daily называет пошлины «политической манипуляцией» и указывает на продуктивные китайско-американские консультации, которые создают дополнительную неопределённость.
importance_reason: Новый раунд пошлин против 14 крупных торговых партнёров, включая Китай и ЕС, с возможным прямым влиянием на торговлю и инфляцию.
market_link: Рост пошлин повышает цены импорта для США и может усилить инфляционное давление; риск для экспортёров сахара и авиатехники (Бразилия), а также для торговых потоков ЕС и Китая; возможна волатильность валют и товарных рынков.

key_facts: The FCA's compensation scheme for mis-sold car finance covers about 12 million car loans, roughly 37% of the total written between April 2007 and November 2024; average expected payout is £829 per mis-sold agreement, with total cost including administrative costs of up to £9.1bn.

The FCA said it found mistakes in how it categorised a small group of loan agreements, with average compensation now estimated between £819 and £839; no compensation will be paid before 2027 due to legal challenges by Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services and Credit Agricole Auto Finance, with the Upper Tribunal hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March 2027.

Complaints have already been filed for about four million agreements; lenders will be told by 18 November (agreements from 1 April 2014 onward, complaints by 30 June 2026) and by 18 January 2027 (earlier agreements, complaints by 31 August).

The scheme follows a 2021 FCA ban on discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs), under which dealers received commission tied to the customer's interest rate; the FCA said commissions in some cases accounted for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.
importance_reason: Multi-billion-pound compensation scheme affecting millions of UK consumers and lenders, with legal delays that carry sector-level financial implications.
market_link: Up to £9.1bn in compensation costs and litigation outcomes may affect UK auto lenders' balance sheets and provisioning, especially captive finance arms of carmakers.

actors: General Sir Gwyn Jenkins (First Sea Lord)
key_facts: The UK signed an £8bn five-year contract with defence firm Babcock to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet.

The MoD said the deal will create 3,000 new jobs and around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles, mainly in Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol; the contract is part of a wider £26bn investment in naval bases announced earlier this year.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the contract structure incentivises Babcock to deliver results, with higher earnings for greater productivity and reduced payment for shortfalls.
The First Sea Lord said the funding is intended to reduce maintenance delays for submarines, which the BBC reports are currently delaying the Royal Navy's operations.
importance_reason: Крупный оборонный контракт с прямым экономическим эффектом на занятость и бюджет, но без прямого влияния на рынки и цены.
